This quintessentially Cuban event offers a fascinating glimpse into a country where politics is woven into every aspect of daily life. Marchers carry placards past images of communist icons such as Marx and Lenin in Plaza de la Revolución. The fact that the entire occasion is carefully stage-managed by party officials only adds to its distinctly Cuban character.

**Havana Carnival (August)**  
One fiesta simply is not enough for a city like Havana, so the Cuban capital hosts two annual carnivals. There is a smaller event in February, which is well worth exploring, but for the full experience, it is best to wait until summer.

Crowds fill the Malecón during the final two weeks of July and the first two weeks of August to hear some of the island’s finest musicians perform al fresco. The final weekend features a colossal parade that makes its way from Habana Vieja to the Malecón in a swirling spectacle of conga lines, daring costumes, music and dancing—accompanied by generous amounts of rum.

Also look out for the “Muñecones,” enormous satirical figures depicting various famous faces, accompanied by the “faroleros,” dancers who twirl brightly colored standards as they parade along the Malecón.

See Carlos Acosta’s Havana »

**The International Havana Ballet Festival (October/November, every other year)**  
This festival brings together international stars and prestigious companies from around the world, while also showcasing the renowned National Ballet of Cuba, which has produced such celebrated figures as Alicia Alonso and Carlos Acosta.

The festival has presented more than 200 world premieres, with performances ranging from classics such as *Swan Lake* to challenging contemporary works. One of its highlights is the range of venues, from the faded grandeur of the Gran Teatro de La Habana, the city’s opera house, to open-air performances in Old Havana, where the subtly lit façades of colonial palaces provide a wonderfully romantic backdrop.

What do you think are Havana’s seasonal highlights? Let us know below.

**Havana Jazz Festival (Winter)**  
Cuban music has played a major role in the development of jazz, with musicians such as Chano Pozo bringing Cuban rhythms to the United States and helping create the fusion known as Latin jazz.

Cuban jazz maestro and five-time Grammy winner Chucho Valdés organizes the festival and is a regular performer, joined by a host of international names. Past editions have featured artists such as Dizzy Gillespie and Max Roach, and although the present-day absence of U.S. stars is notable, it is more than offset by an impressive contingent of Latin American talent.

Performances take place at the Hotel Riviera, Casa de la Cultura Plaza, Teatro Nacional de Cuba, Teatro Amadeo Roldán and various smoky clubs. Although the jazz festival is usually held in December, the 2009 event took place in February, so if you are planning a visit, be sure to check the dates well in advance.

**The Festival of New Latin American Cinema (December)**  
This 10-day festival is one of the largest events in Latin American film, a region currently producing some of the finest cinema in the world. Movie enthusiasts from across the island flock to see an impressive selection of films, ranging from Spanish-language blockbusters to obscure art-house works.

Even if your Spanish is not strong enough to fully follow the films being shown, the festival still offers the chance to spot a few celebrities. Past attendees have included Robert De Niro, Robert Redford, Jack Nicholson, Steven Spielberg and Pedro Almodóvar.

# Havana’s biggest festivals: When Cuba’s capital turns into a street-wide celebration

Havana is rarely quiet. On any given night, music leaks from colonial doorways, neighbors pull chairs onto sidewalks, and vintage cars rumble past sea-sprayed facades along the Malecón. But several times a year, the Cuban capital shifts into a higher gear, when politics, dance, cinema, ballet and jazz draw crowds into theaters, plazas and avenues across the city.

For travelers, Havana’s major annual festivals offer a revealing way to experience the city — not just as a postcard of pastel architecture and mojitos, but as a living cultural capital with deep African, Caribbean, European and revolutionary traditions.

Here are the big events worth planning a trip around.

## May Day: Havana’s mass gathering in Revolution Square

Havana’s May Day celebrations are among the largest public events in Cuba, centered on Plaza de la Revolución, the vast square watched over by the iconic steel outlines of Che Guevara and Camilo Cienfuegos.

Held on May 1, International Workers’ Day is both a political event and a national spectacle. In the early morning, crowds gather with flags, banners and music as workers, students and community groups march through the plaza. The atmosphere can feel part parade, part rally, part national ritual.

For visitors, it’s an opportunity to witness a defining image of modern Cuba: collective, symbolic and highly choreographed, but also full of everyday energy. Arrive early, expect heavy crowds and limited transport near the square, and bring water — Havana’s May heat can be intense even before midday.

## Havana Carnival: Drums, dancers and parades by the sea

Carnival in Havana is not as internationally famous as those in Rio or Trinidad, but it is one of the city’s most vibrant street celebrations. Usually held in summer, often around July or August, the event brings comparsas — neighborhood dance troupes — onto the streets with drums, sequins, floats and a distinctly Afro-Cuban pulse.

Much of the action traditionally unfolds along the Malecón, Havana’s beloved seaside promenade. At night, the waterfront becomes a grandstand for music, dancing and street food, with locals and visitors lining the route as performers move past in waves of color and percussion.

The roots of Cuban carnival stretch back through colonial-era festivals, African traditions and working-class neighborhoods. In Havana, that history remains visible in the rhythms, costumes and call-and-response energy of the crowds.

For travelers, this is one of the best times to see Havana outdoors and unfiltered. Bring cash, wear comfortable shoes and be ready for late nights — carnival does not run on a quiet schedule.

## International Ballet Festival of Havana: Cuba’s classical calling card

Cuba’s ballet tradition is one of the country’s great cultural surprises for many first-time visitors. The International Ballet Festival of Havana, founded in 1960 and closely associated with legendary Cuban ballerina Alicia Alonso, is one of the oldest ballet festivals in the world.

Typically held every two years, the festival draws Cuban and international dancers to some of Havana’s most elegant venues, including the Gran Teatro de La Habana Alicia Alonso, a lavish landmark near the Capitolio. Performances range from classical repertoire to contemporary works, often featuring the renowned Ballet Nacional de Cuba.

The event reveals a different side of Havana: formal, theatrical and deeply proud of its artistic institutions. Even travelers who don’t usually plan trips around ballet may find the experience memorable, if only for the setting — gilded interiors, old-world glamour and audiences that treat ballet as a national treasure.

Tickets can sell quickly for major performances, so planning ahead is wise. Dress codes are not always rigid, but Cubans often dress smartly for the theater.

## Havana Jazz Festival: The city in improvisation mode

Havana’s jazz scene is one of the most exciting in the Americas, blending bebop, Afro-Cuban percussion, rumba, son, timba and experimental sounds. The Havana Jazz Festival — officially the Jazz Plaza International Festival — usually takes place in January, turning the city into a magnet for musicians from Cuba and abroad.

Concerts are held in theaters, cultural centers and clubs, with major performances complemented by late-night jam sessions. The result is a festival that feels both highly professional and spontaneous. A formal evening concert may be followed by a small-room session where world-class musicians trade solos into the early hours.

Cuba has produced an extraordinary number of jazz greats, and the festival is a chance to hear the island’s musical sophistication up close. Expect complex rhythms, powerhouse brass, virtuosic piano and a crowd that knows exactly when a solo catches fire.

For visitors, the jazz festival is also a strong reason to explore beyond the most obvious tourist haunts. Venues such as Teatro Nacional, Casa de la Cultura locations and intimate music clubs can all be part of the circuit, depending on the year’s program.

## International Festival of New Latin American Cinema: Havana on screen

Every December, Havana becomes one of Latin America’s great film capitals during the International Festival of New Latin American Cinema. Founded in 1979, the festival was created to showcase films from Latin America and the Caribbean, with an emphasis on regional storytelling, social themes and independent voices.

Screenings take place across the city, including at historic cinemas that recall Havana’s long love affair with the movies. The program typically includes feature films, documentaries, shorts, retrospectives and panels, drawing directors, actors, critics and cinephiles from across the region.

The atmosphere is lively and democratic: students, filmmakers, locals and travelers line up for screenings, debate films in café courtyards and move between cinemas with festival schedules in hand. Spanish is the dominant language, and many films may not have English subtitles, but for cinema lovers, the energy alone is worth it.

The festival also offers a window into contemporary Latin American concerns — migration, memory, inequality, identity, politics and family — seen through the lens of filmmakers from across the hemisphere.

## Planning a festival trip to Havana

Havana’s festival calendar rewards travelers who plan ahead but stay flexible. Dates can vary from year to year, and schedules are sometimes announced closer to the event than visitors may expect. Before booking, check official festival channels, Cuban cultural institutions or reputable travel operators for updated information.

Accommodation fills quickly during major events, particularly around the jazz and film festivals, so it’s smart to reserve early. Staying in neighborhoods such as Habana Vieja, Vedado or Centro Habana puts visitors close to many venues and nightlife options.

Transport can be unpredictable during large gatherings, especially May Day and Carnival. Walking, pre-arranged taxis and patience are often the best tools. Carry cash, as card payments are not always reliable, and keep essentials like water, sunscreen and a portable phone charger on hand.

Most of all, come ready to participate rather than simply observe. In Havana, culture rarely stays behind a velvet rope. It spills into plazas, theaters, cinemas, clubs and seawalls — and, during festival season, it can feel as if the whole city has joined the performance.

## Seasonal Highlights in Havana, Cuba

Havana’s calendar is filled with music, dance, film, religious traditions, and street celebrations. While the city is lively year-round, certain months bring major festivals that offer visitors a deeper look at Cuban culture.

### January–February: Jazz and Culture Season
**Havana International Jazz Plaza Festival** usually takes place in **January** and draws renowned Cuban and international jazz musicians to theaters, clubs, and open-air venues across the city. Visitors can expect world-class performances, jam sessions, and a festive atmosphere in neighborhoods like Vedado and Old Havana.

In **February**, Havana often hosts cultural fairs, concerts, and art events, making it a pleasant time to explore the city in cooler, drier weather.

### March–April: Dance, Theater, and Spring Festivals
Spring is a great time for performing arts. Havana’s theaters and cultural centers often feature ballet, contemporary dance, and theater programs during these months. Around **Easter**, while Cuba is not as openly religious in public celebrations as some Latin American countries, visitors may still find church services and small local observances.

This is also a good season for walking tours, rooftop evenings, and exploring the Malecón before summer heat arrives.

### May: Cuban Music and Community Celebrations
**Cubadisco**, Cuba’s major music awards and festival, is typically held in **May**. It celebrates Cuban recording artists across genres such as son, salsa, trova, jazz, and timba. Expect concerts, award ceremonies, panel discussions, and live performances throughout Havana.

May also brings **International Workers’ Day on May 1**, marked by large public gatherings and parades, especially around Plaza de la Revolución.

### July: Carnival and Summer Festivities
Havana’s **Carnival** traditionally takes place in **July or early August**, filling the city with parades, comparsas, drum groups, dancers, costumes, and street food. While Santiago de Cuba is better known for carnival, Havana’s version offers a lively urban celebration along major avenues and seaside areas.

Summer is hot and humid, so visitors should plan for evening events, carry water, and expect a high-energy local crowd.

### August: Festival of Fire and Afro-Cuban Traditions
Although the famous **Fiesta del Fuego** is held in Santiago de Cuba in July, Havana also hosts Afro-Cuban music, rumba, and religious-cultural performances throughout the summer. Visitors interested in Afro-Cuban traditions can look for rumba gatherings, folkloric dance shows, and community events in venues such as Callejón de Hamel.

### September–October: Quieter Months and Cultural Openings
September is one of Havana’s quieter travel periods due to heat, humidity, and the possibility of storms. However, it can be a rewarding time for fewer crowds and more local experiences.

By **October**, the arts calendar begins to pick up again. Galleries, theaters, and music venues launch new programs, and the city’s nightlife becomes more active as the weather gradually improves.

### November: Havana Anniversary and Performing Arts
**Havana’s founding anniversary**, celebrated around **November 16**, brings historical and cultural events, especially in Old Havana. Visitors may encounter concerts, exhibitions, guided walks, and ceremonies connected to the city’s colonial heritage.

Every other year, Havana also hosts the **International Ballet Festival of Havana**, usually in **October or November**. It is one of the world’s oldest ballet festivals and features Cuban and international dancers performing in grand venues such as the Gran Teatro de La Habana.

### December: Film, Festivities, and Year-End Celebrations
The **International Festival of New Latin American Cinema** is one of Havana’s most important cultural events and usually takes place in **December**. Film screenings, premieres, talks, and awards attract filmmakers and cinema lovers from across Latin America and beyond.

December also brings holiday energy to the city. Christmas is generally celebrated more quietly than in some countries, but visitors can enjoy special meals, live music, decorated hotels and restaurants, and New Year’s Eve celebrations along the Malecón or in Havana’s music venues.

## Best Time to Visit for Events
For cultural festivals, the best months are **January, May, July, November, and December**. Travelers seeking cooler weather and a packed arts calendar often prefer **November through March**, while those interested in street celebrations and summer nightlife may enjoy **July and August**.

Event dates in Havana can shift from year to year, so visitors should check local listings, hotel concierges, cultural centers, and official tourism sources before traveling.

# Havana’s best annual events

Havana doesn’t need much help putting on a show. On any given night, music spills from balconies in Centro Habana, couples drift through plazas to the sound of son, and the Malecón becomes the city’s front-row seat to sunset.

But time your visit around one of the Cuban capital’s major annual events, and the city seems to turn up the volume. From jazz marathons and ballet galas to street parades, film screenings and rum-fueled celebrations, Havana’s festival calendar offers a vivid route into the island’s culture.

Here are some of the best annual events to plan a trip around.

## Havana International Jazz Festival

Usually held in January, the Havana International Jazz Festival is one of the city’s great cultural calling cards. Founded in the late 1970s, it draws Cuban virtuosos and international performers for concerts, jam sessions and late-night improvisations across the capital.

Venues range from grand theaters to smaller clubs where the atmosphere is more intimate and the solos can run deep into the night. For visitors, the festival is a reminder that Cuban jazz is not a museum piece but a living, constantly evolving conversation between Afro-Cuban rhythms, bebop, salsa, classical music and global sounds.

## Havana Biennial

The Havana Biennial is the city’s biggest contemporary art event, typically staged every two or three years rather than annually, but it remains one of the most important dates on Havana’s cultural calendar.

During the biennial, galleries, museums, public spaces and colonial courtyards become showcases for artists from Cuba, Latin America, the Caribbean, Africa and beyond. Installations spill into the streets, conversations unfold in studios, and the city itself becomes part of the exhibition.

For travelers, it’s one of the best ways to explore Havana beyond its postcard views, revealing a capital that is intellectually restless, politically layered and visually bold.

## International Ballet Festival of Havana

Havana’s ballet tradition is legendary, and this festival is its grandest stage. The International Ballet Festival of Havana, founded by Cuban ballet icon Alicia Alonso, usually takes place every two years, bringing elite dancers and companies to the city’s elegant theaters.

The main performances are often held at the Gran Teatro de La Habana Alicia Alonso, one of the capital’s architectural jewels. Expect a mix of classical repertoire, Cuban choreography and international guest appearances. Even for those who don’t normally seek out ballet on vacation, the festival offers a glimpse into one of Cuba’s most cherished artistic institutions.

## Havana Film Festival

Every December, the Festival Internacional del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano turns Havana into one of the region’s most important film capitals. Since 1979, the festival has championed Latin American cinema, screening features, documentaries, shorts and experimental works from across the continent.

For locals, it’s a beloved tradition: long lines outside cinemas, animated post-screening debates and packed theaters where audiences respond with unmistakable Cuban candor. For visitors, it’s a rare chance to see the region through its own filmmakers’ eyes, far from the usual tourist lens.

## Habanos Festival

For cigar aficionados, the Habanos Festival is the ultimate pilgrimage. Usually held in late February or early March, it celebrates Cuba’s most famous export with tastings, factory tours, plantation visits, auctions and gala dinners.

The event attracts collectors, distributors and enthusiasts from around the world. While much of the programming is geared toward industry insiders and serious cigar lovers, the festival also offers a window into the craftsmanship behind Cuba’s premium cigars, from tobacco fields in Pinar del Río to the rolling tables of Havana’s historic factories.

## Havana Carnival

Cuba’s biggest carnival celebrations are often associated with Santiago de Cuba, but Havana has its own festive summer blowout. Typically held in July or August, Havana Carnival brings comparsas, conga lines, floats and percussion to the capital’s streets and seafront.

The Malecón often becomes the center of the action, with food stalls, music and crowds gathering after dark. It’s noisy, colorful and unapologetically communal — less polished spectacle than neighborhood celebration, and all the better for it.

## International Book Fair of Havana

Each February, the International Book Fair of Havana transforms the city into a sprawling literary gathering, with its main events traditionally held at the Fortaleza de San Carlos de la Cabaña, the 18th-century fortress overlooking the bay.

Publishers, writers and readers come together for book launches, panel discussions, readings and cultural performances. The setting is part of the appeal: visitors can browse books from inside stone ramparts while looking back across the water toward Old Havana’s domes and towers.

The fair later travels to other Cuban provinces, but its Havana opening is the main event.

## Fiesta del Fuego and Afro-Cuban cultural events

While the famous Fiesta del Fuego is held in Santiago de Cuba, Havana hosts a wide range of Afro-Cuban religious, musical and cultural events throughout the year, especially in neighborhoods where rumba, Yoruba traditions and community performance remain deeply rooted.

Visitors may encounter rumba gatherings, folkloric dance performances and ceremonies connected to Afro-Cuban spiritual life. Some are public, others are private or community-based, so respectful participation is essential. When experienced thoughtfully, these events offer a powerful understanding of the African heritage that shapes Cuban music, dance and identity.

## International Festival of New Latin American Cinema

Though often simply called the Havana Film Festival, this December event deserves emphasis for the way it takes over the city. Havana’s cinemas fill with students, critics, directors and everyday moviegoers, many clutching printed schedules and plotting ambitious screening routes.

Unlike red-carpet festivals built around celebrity culture, Havana’s version feels intensely democratic. The audience is the star: opinionated, passionate and ready to applaud, argue or laugh in unison. It’s one of the most atmospheric times to be in the capital.

## New Year’s Eve and Triumph of the Revolution

New Year’s Eve in Havana coincides with one of Cuba’s most significant national dates: January 1, the anniversary of the Triumph of the Revolution. The result is a holiday period that blends family gatherings, public celebrations and political commemoration.

Visitors will find restaurants and music venues hosting special dinners and parties, while many Cubans mark the night at home with relatives, roast pork and rum. At midnight, the city can feel both festive and reflective — a place where personal ritual and national history meet.

## A city that celebrates in rhythm

Havana’s best events are not sealed off from the city around them. They spill into taxis, cafés, seawalls and late-night conversations. A jazz festival performance may lead to a rumba session. A film screening may end with a debate over coffee. A carnival parade may become an invitation to dance with strangers.

That is the pleasure of planning around Havana’s calendar: the official event is only the beginning. The real festival is often the city itself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lively overview of Havana’s cultural calendar, covering politics, music, dance, ballet, jazz, rum, carnival parades, and cinema.
counterfactuals.output:
Havana’s cultural calendar is as dense, noisy, and irresistible as the city itself: a year-round swirl of revolutionary pageantry, late-night music, dance floors, ballet stages, jazz clubs, rum-soaked festivals, carnival drums, and cinema under tropical skies. Dates can shift from year to year, but the rhythm of the city is remarkably reliable.

## January: Revolution, jazz, and a city shaking off the holidays

The year opens with politics at full volume. **January 1**, the anniversary of the **Triumph of the Cuban Revolution**, is one of the country’s most symbolic dates, marked by official ceremonies, speeches, concerts, and patriotic programming. Havana’s plazas, museums, and cultural institutions often lean into revolutionary history, with exhibitions, tributes, and public events.

January is also one of the best months for music lovers. The **Havana International Jazz Festival**, usually held in January, brings Cuban virtuosos together with musicians from across the world. Expect everything from formal concerts in theaters to jam sessions that stretch into the small hours, with Afro-Cuban rhythms, bebop, Latin jazz, and experimental fusion all colliding in true Havana style.

## February–March: Books, trova, and street-level culture

Early in the year, Havana often hosts the **International Book Fair**, centered around the historic **Fortaleza de San Carlos de la Cabaña**. It is not just a literary event; it is a social ritual. Families, students, publishers, poets, politicians, and street vendors all gather in a festive atmosphere where books share space with concerts, panel discussions, and food stalls.

This is also a fine season for **trova**, the Cuban singer-songwriter tradition. In intimate venues and cultural centers, you can hear songs that blend romance, politics, melancholy, and sharp social observation.

## April–May: Dance, son, and the city’s musical pulse

Spring in Havana belongs to movement. Dance schools, cultural houses, and theaters stage performances ranging from folkloric Afro-Cuban dance to contemporary choreography. The city’s music scene is constant, but this is a wonderful time to seek out **son cubano**, salsa, timba, and rumba.

For rumba, head toward neighborhood gatherings, cultural venues, or the famous **Callejón de Hamel**, where Afro-Cuban religion, percussion, mural art, and dance all meet in a colorful Sunday ritual. It is part performance, part community celebration, and part spiritual inheritance.

## July: Revolution Day and carnival season

July brings one of Cuba’s major political commemorations: **July 26**, the **Day of National Rebellion**, marking the 1953 attack on the Moncada Barracks. While the central national ceremony may take place in different provinces, Havana still marks the occasion with official events, concerts, banners, televised speeches, and patriotic cultural programming.

Late July and August are also when the city loosens its collar. **Havana Carnival** fills the Malecón and surrounding avenues with conga lines, comparsas, drums, costumes, floats, and a thundering sense of public joy. It is not a polished parade in the purely tourist sense; it is sweaty, crowded, loud, and deeply Cuban. The pulse of the drums seems to bounce off the sea wall.

## August: Rum, heat, and nights by the Malecón

August in Havana is hot, but culturally alive. Carnival energy lingers, and the city’s nightlife spills outdoors. Rum is never far from the picture. Whether in a classic **mojito**, a **daiquiri**, or a neat pour of aged Cuban rum, Havana’s drinking culture is bound up with music, conversation, and myth.

Visitors often make the pilgrimage to bars associated with Hemingway, but rum culture goes far beyond the old postcard circuit. Look for tastings, cocktail events, hotel bars with live music, and casual neighborhood spots where the soundtrack might be bolero, reggaetón, salsa, or a baseball game on television.

## October–November: Ballet, theater, and high culture in grand style

Havana has one of Latin America’s great ballet traditions, shaped by the legacy of **Alicia Alonso** and the **Ballet Nacional de Cuba**. The **International Ballet Festival of Havana**, traditionally held every two years, is a jewel of the calendar. Performances take place in elegant theaters, often including the magnificent **Gran Teatro de La Habana Alicia Alonso**.

Even outside festival years, ballet remains central to the city’s cultural identity. Havana takes dance seriously: audiences are knowledgeable, students line up for affordable seats, and the atmosphere can feel both glamorous and democratic.

This period is also rich in theater, contemporary dance, visual arts, and concerts, as the cooler months bring a fuller cultural schedule.

## December: Cinema, nostalgia, and the year’s grand finale

December belongs to film. The **International Festival of New Latin American Cinema** is one of Havana’s most important cultural events, drawing filmmakers, critics, students, and cinephiles from across the region. Screenings take place in classic cinemas around the city, and the mood is both intellectual and celebratory.

The festival showcases Latin American political cinema, documentaries, social dramas, experimental work, and crowd-pleasing features. In Havana, cinema is never just entertainment; it is conversation, ideology, memory, and debate.

As the year closes, Havana folds Christmas, New Year’s Eve, and revolutionary anniversary preparations into one extended season of family meals, music, rum, and public festivity.

## The constant soundtrack: music everywhere

Beyond the formal calendar, Havana’s real culture happens nightly. Music pours out of courtyards, clubs, hotel lobbies, rehearsal rooms, private restaurants, and open-air venues. You can hear:

- **Son cubano** in traditional clubs  
- **Rumba** in community spaces and Afro-Cuban cultural gatherings  
- **Timba and salsa** in dance halls  
- **Bolero** in intimate bars  
- **Jazz** in dedicated clubs and festival stages  
- **Reggaetón and reparto** from passing cars, phones, and neighborhood parties  

The city does not treat music as background. It is a language of identity, flirtation, politics, survival, and joy.

## A calendar of politics and pleasure

What makes Havana’s cultural year so distinctive is the way politics and pleasure overlap. Revolutionary anniversaries come with concerts. Film festivals host ideological debates. Carnival parades carry African, Spanish, Caribbean, and socialist-era layers of history. Ballet can feel aristocratic in setting but popular in spirit. Rum is both a tourist emblem and a daily social lubricant.

Havana’s calendar is not tidy. It is improvised, sometimes underfunded, frequently brilliant, and always alive. To follow it is to discover a city where culture is not confined to museums or theaters: it moves through the streets, argues in cafés, dances on the Malecón, sings in courtyards, and keeps time with the drums.

## 10 Annual Havana Events Worth Planning a Trip Around

*Dates in Cuba can shift from year to year, so treat the timing below as a reliable seasonal guide—and confirm the official program before booking.*

---

### 1. **Festival Internacional Jazz Plaza**
**When:** Usually **January**  
**Where:** **Teatro Nacional de Cuba**, **Casa de la Cultura de Plaza**, **Fábrica de Arte Cubano**, and other Havana stages  
**Why go:** Havana becomes a jazz city in full swing—late-night jam sessions, packed theaters, and musicians drifting from formal concerts to informal descarga sessions.

**Famous names:** The festival is closely associated with Cuban jazz giants such as **Chucho Valdés**, **Roberto Fonseca**, **Daymé Arocena**, and **Aldo López-Gavilán**, and has welcomed international artists including **Arturo O’Farrill** and other major Latin-jazz performers.

**Atmosphere:** Sophisticated but lively—think smoky-club energy, virtuoso piano solos, rum cocktails, and crowds who really know their music.

---

### 2. **Festival del Habano**
**When:** Usually **late February**  
**Where:** **Palacio de Convenciones**, **Pabexpo**, cigar factories, tobacco farms, and gala venues around Havana  
**Why go:** This is the world’s biggest celebration of Cuban cigars, drawing collectors, luxury travelers, sommeliers, and cigar-industry insiders.

**Famous names:** While it’s less about pop performers and more about cigar culture, the festival’s gala nights often feature major Cuban musicians and orchestras. Past editions have included high-profile musical guests and celebrity attendees from the worlds of film, business, and sport.

**Atmosphere:** Polished and exclusive—factory tours by day, rum-and-cigar pairings by evening, and glamorous gala dinners where humidors can sell for staggering prices.

---

### 3. **Feria Internacional del Libro de La Habana**
**When:** Usually **February**  
**Where:** **Fortaleza de San Carlos de la Cabaña**, with events also at bookstores, cultural centers, and universities  
**Why go:** One of Cuba’s most beloved cultural events, the Havana International Book Fair fills the old fortress across the bay with readers, publishers, students, families, and food stalls.

**Famous names:** The fair regularly hosts Cuban and Latin American writers, intellectuals, poets, historians, and visiting delegations from the guest-of-honor country.

**Atmosphere:** Warm, crowded, and family-friendly—part literary festival, part school outing, part street fair, with sweeping views back toward Old Havana.

---

### 4. **Fiesta del Tambor “Guillermo Barreto”**
**When:** Usually **March**  
**Where:** **Teatro Mella**, **Casa de la Música**, cultural centers, and Havana music venues  
**Why go:** This is Havana’s great percussion festival, dedicated to Afro-Cuban rhythm, rumba, timba, jazz, and dance.

**Famous names:** The event has featured or honored legendary Cuban percussionists and musicians such as **José Luis “Changuito” Quintana**, **Yaroldy Abreu**, **Horacio “El Negro” Hernández**, and leading rumba and timba groups.

**Atmosphere:** Electric and physical—you don’t just hear the drums, you feel them. Expect dancers in the aisles, rumba circles, and late-night concerts that run hot.

---

### 5. **Havana World Music**
**When:** Usually **March**  
**Where:** Often held at outdoor venues such as **Ciudad Deportiva** or other large cultural spaces in Havana  
**Why go:** A younger, festival-style event bringing together Cuban fusion, Afrobeat, reggae, funk, electronic music, and global sounds.

**Famous names:** Founded and curated by Cuban singer **Eme Alfonso**, the festival has highlighted artists such as **Cimafunk**, **Telmary**, **Interactivo**, and emerging international acts.

**Atmosphere:** Youthful, open-air, and stylish—more food trucks and festival fashion than formal theater seating. A great pick for travelers who want contemporary Havana rather than postcard nostalgia.

---

### 6. **Cubadisco**
**When:** Usually **May**  
**Where:** **Teatro Karl Marx**, **Teatro Nacional**, recording studios, cultural centers, and concert halls  
**Why go:** Cuba’s major music-industry festival and awards event, celebrating recordings, concerts, and the breadth of Cuban music—from son and trova to classical, jazz, reggaetón, and fusion.

**Famous names:** Past editions have involved leading Cuban artists across generations, including figures connected to **Los Van Van**, **Omara Portuondo**, **Chucho Valdés**, **Adalberto Álvarez**, and newer Cuban music scenes.

**Atmosphere:** A mix of awards-show glamour and serious music appreciation, with concerts that can range from symphonic to dance-floor-ready.

---

### 7. **Carnaval de La Habana**
**When:** Usually **July or August**, often on weekends  
**Where:** Along the **Malecón**, especially near the waterfront parade route  
**Why go:** Havana’s carnival is all about comparsas, conga lines, floats, costumes, street food, and loud percussion echoing off the sea wall.

**Famous names:** The stars here are the traditional **comparsas** and neighborhood dance troupes, along with popular Cuban bands that may perform in associated concerts.

**Atmosphere:** Hot, noisy, salty, and joyful. Locals crowd the Malecón with families, friends, bottles of rum, and street snacks. It’s one of the best times to see Havana celebrating outdoors.

---

### 8. **Festival Internacional de Teatro de La Habana**
**When:** Usually **October**, though schedules can vary  
**Where:** **Teatro Nacional**, **Teatro Mella**, **Teatro Trianón**, **Sala Adolfo Llauradó**, and other stages  
**Why go:** A major performing-arts event featuring Cuban theater companies and international troupes, with drama, dance-theater, experimental work, and street performances.

**Famous names:** The festival often includes acclaimed Cuban theater groups such as **Teatro El Público**, **Argos Teatro**, and other notable Latin American and European companies.

**Atmosphere:** Creative and cosmopolitan. Some shows are formal and ticketed; others spill into public spaces, giving visitors a look at Havana’s intellectual and artistic circles.

---

### 9. **Marabana / Maracuba**
**When:** Usually **November**  
**Where:** Starts and finishes around central Havana routes, often passing landmarks such as the **Malecón**, **Paseo del Prado**, **Vedado**, and historic districts  
**Why go:** Havana’s signature running event includes marathon, half-marathon, and shorter races, attracting Cuban and international runners.

**Famous names:** The draw is more athletic than celebrity-driven, though top Cuban and international distance runners often participate.

**Atmosphere:** Surprisingly festive—locals cheer from balconies, runners pass faded mansions and ocean views, and the city feels like an open-air course through history.

---

### 10. **Festival Internacional del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano**
**When:** Usually **December**  
**Where:** **Cine Charles Chaplin**, **Cine Yara**, **Cine 23 y 12**, **Hotel Nacional de Cuba**, and other cinemas and cultural venues  
**Why go:** One of Latin America’s most important film festivals, this event brings directors, actors, critics, students, and movie lovers to Havana for premieres, retrospectives, and packed screenings.

**Famous names:** The festival has long been linked with leading Latin American filmmakers and has honored figures such as **Gabriel García Márquez**, who helped inspire the region’s film movement, as well as major directors from Cuba, Mexico, Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and beyond.

**Atmosphere:** Cinephile and buzzing—long lines outside theaters, animated debates after screenings, and a sense that everyone in Havana is suddenly talking about film.

---

## Quick Planning Tip

If you want **music and nightlife**, aim for **January to March**. For **street energy**, come during **Carnaval in summer**. For **film and culture**, **December** is hard to beat. Havana’s event calendar is rich, but schedules can be fluid—always check official festival pages or local cultural listings close to your travel dates.
